name: Pharynx
func: The throat: a muscular tube behind the nose and mouth shared by air and food. It carries air to the larynx and pushes swallowed food into the esophagus, with tonsils guarding the entrance against germs.

levels.kid:
The **pharynx** is your **throat**. It's a tube at the back of your nose and mouth. Open your mouth wide in a mirror and say "ahh": the pink wall you see at the very back is part of it!

It's a shared hallway. Air goes through it on the way to your lungs, and food goes through it on the way to your tummy. At the bottom, the hallway splits: air goes to the front tube (the windpipe) and food goes to the back tube (the food pipe).

When you swallow, muscles in the pharynx squeeze in a wave, pushing food down, and your airway shuts for a moment so the food doesn't go the wrong way.

Your **tonsils** live here too. They're little guards that catch germs coming in through your mouth and nose.
levels.hs:
The **pharynx** is a muscular tube about **12–14 cm long**, running from the **base of the skull** down to the lower edge of the **cricoid cartilage** (about **C6**), where it becomes the **esophagus**. It lies in front of the cervical vertebrae and the prevertebral muscles, behind the nose, mouth and larynx. The great vessels of the neck (carotid arteries, internal jugular veins) and the vagus nerve run in the **carotid sheaths** beside it.

It has three parts:
- **Nasopharynx**: behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate. It contains the openings of the **auditory (Eustachian) tubes**, which connect to the middle ears, and the **adenoids** (pharyngeal tonsil). It carries only air.
- **Oropharynx**: behind the mouth, from the soft palate to the epiglottis. It holds the **palatine tonsils** (the ones people mean when they say "tonsils") and the **lingual tonsil** at the back of the tongue. Air and food both pass here.
- **Laryngopharynx (hypopharynx)**: behind the larynx, from the epiglottis to C6, leading into the esophagus.

The tonsils form a ring of lymphoid tissue, **Waldeyer's ring**, which samples germs entering through the nose and mouth.
levels.college:
The pharyngeal wall has an outer, roughly circular layer of three overlapping **constrictor muscles** (superior, middle, inferior), stacked like paper cups, and a thinner inner longitudinal layer of **stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus**, which shorten and lift the pharynx during swallowing.

The **inferior constrictor** has two parts: the oblique **thyropharyngeus** and the horizontal **cricopharyngeus**. The cricopharyngeus is the main component of the **upper esophageal sphincter (UES)**, tonically closed at rest. Between the two parts at the back is a weak spot, **Killian's dehiscence**.

**Nerves**: the **pharyngeal plexus**, formed mainly by the **vagus (CN X)** and **glossopharyngeal (CN IX)** nerves, plus sympathetic fibres. CN X (via the plexus) supplies almost all pharyngeal muscles; the exception is **stylopharyngeus**, supplied by **CN IX**. Sensation of the oropharynx, including the posterior third of the tongue and the tonsils, is via CN IX, which carries the afferent limb of the **gag reflex**; CN X is the efferent limb. The nasopharynx gets sensory supply from the maxillary nerve (CN V2); the laryngopharynx from the vagus.

**Swallowing** has three phases: **oral** (voluntary push back by the tongue), **pharyngeal** (an involuntary reflex taking under about a second: soft palate seals the nasopharynx, larynx rises and closes, constrictors squeeze, UES opens) and **esophageal**.

The **piriform fossae** (recesses on each side of the laryngeal inlet) and the **valleculae** (between tongue base and epiglottis) are where food residue and fish bones commonly lodge.

Behind the pharynx lies the **retropharyngeal space**, a potential space that runs from the skull base into the chest, a route for infection to spread down to the mediastinum.
levels.phd:
The pharyngeal swallow is driven by a **central pattern generator** in the medulla. A **dorsal swallowing group** in and around the **nucleus tractus solitarius** receives sensory input (CN V, IX, X, especially the internal laryngeal nerve) and organises the sequence; a **ventral group** near the **nucleus ambiguus** distributes commands to motor neurons. The sequence runs the same way regardless of what triggered it, though bolus size and consistency modulate its timing and force. Cortical areas (including the insula and primary sensorimotor cortex) start the voluntary oral phase and adjust the reflex, with bilateral but often asymmetric representation, which explains why many people recover swallowing after a one-sided stroke as the other hemisphere reorganises.

Breathing and swallowing are tightly coupled: a **swallow apnoea** briefly halts breathing, and most healthy adults swallow in the expiratory phase and resume with expiration, lowering aspiration risk. This coordination often fails in Parkinson disease and COPD.

**Embryology**: the pharynx comes from the **pharyngeal (branchial) apparatus**. The pharyngeal pouches give rise to the auditory tube and middle ear (1st), the **palatine tonsil crypts** (2nd), the inferior parathyroids and thymus (3rd) and the superior parathyroids and ultimobranchial body (4th). The constrictors come from arches 4 and 6, matching their vagal supply; stylopharyngeus from arch 3, matching CN IX.

Tonsillar **crypts** are lined by a specialised **reticulated epithelium** containing M-like cells that transport antigens to underlying germinal centres, making the tonsils inductive sites for mucosal immunity and IgA production.

The nasopharyngeal epithelium is the site of **Epstein–Barr virus**-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma, with a striking geographic distribution (very common in southern China), an active area of viral oncology research.
levels.expert:
**Exam**: inspect the oropharynx with a tongue depressor and light. The **uvula** should hang in the midline. With a unilateral **vagus (CN X) lesion**, the uvula deviates **away from** the lesion as the intact side's muscles pull it, and the soft palate on the weak side doesn't rise. The **gag reflex** tests CN IX (sensory) and CN X (motor), though many healthy people have a weak gag.

**Dysphagia** assessment: a bedside water-swallow screen, then a **videofluoroscopic swallow study** or **fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES)**. Watch for **silent aspiration** (no cough), common after stroke and brainstem injury.

**Neuro relevance**: **bulbar palsy** (lower motor neuron, as in motor neuron disease or lateral medullary syndrome) causes a weak palate, absent gag and wasted tongue; **pseudobulbar palsy** (bilateral upper motor neuron damage) causes a brisk gag and jaw jerk with emotional lability. Myasthenia gravis causes fatiguable swallowing. Swallow problems drive aspiration pneumonia, a major cause of death after stroke.

**Infections**: **peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)**: severe one-sided throat pain, trismus, muffled "hot potato" voice and the uvula pushed **away**; treated by drainage plus antibiotics. **Retropharyngeal abscess** in children shows widened prevertebral soft tissue on a lateral neck X-ray and can spread to the mediastinum.

**Zenker's (pharyngeal pouch) diverticulum** herniates through Killian's dehiscence in older adults: regurgitation of undigested food, bad breath and a gurgling neck. A barium swallow confirms it; treatment is endoscopic or open division of cricopharyngeus.

**Tumours**: nasopharyngeal carcinoma may present with a one-sided middle-ear effusion (blocked Eustachian tube), neck nodes, or cranial nerve palsies from skull-base invasion. Oropharyngeal cancer is linked to smoking, and a growing share is driven by a viral infection of the tonsil tissue. The transoral and **endoscopic endonasal** routes to the skull base pass through the pharynx.

keyPoints: Throat tube from skull base to C6, continuous with esophagus
Waldeyer's ring of tonsils guards the entrance
Constrictors supplied by CN X; stylopharyngeus by CN IX
Gag reflex: CN IX in, CN X out
Uvula deviates away from a CN X lesion

test.q: Which part of the pharynx contains the openings of the Eustachian tubes?
test.explain: The auditory tubes open into the nasopharynx, linking it to the middle ear.

test.q: The only pharyngeal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve is ______.
test.explain: Stylopharyngeus comes from the 3rd pharyngeal arch, the arch of CN IX.

test.q: A patient's uvula deviates to the right. Which vagus nerve is damaged?
test.explain: The intact right side pulls the uvula toward itself, so it points away from the damaged left vagus.

test.q: A pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) pushes out through which weak spot?
test.explain: Killian's dehiscence lies between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor.

test.q: The ring of lymphoid tissue (tonsils and adenoids) around the pharynx is called ______ ring.
test.explain: Waldeyer's ring includes the adenoid, tubal, palatine and lingual tonsils.
